name: Behavioral Activation
description: Systematic scheduling of meaningful activities to counteract depression-related withdrawal and anhedonia.
mechanism: Breaks avoidance cycle; increases behavioral momentum and social contact; builds positive reinforcement
steps: Create a list of activities you find or used to find meaningful (hobby, sports, time with friends, learning)
Rate each activity by difficulty (1-10) and by how much it would help your mood if completed
Start with low-difficulty activities this week (even 15-30 min counts)
Schedule one activity daily, tracking your mood before and after
Gradually add more challenging activities as you build momentum
Notice patterns: which activities help most? When do you have most energy?
Adjust schedule based on what works for your depression
bestFor: Teens struggling with motivation or feeling like 'nothing matters'
Those withdrawn from activities they used to enjoy
Those resistant to talk therapy initially

name: Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) - Youth Adapted
description: Gradual exposure to feared situations combined with deliberately NOT engaging in anxiety-reducing behaviors (compulsions). Highly effective for OCD, social anxiety, and specific phobias.
effectiveness: 75-85% for anxiety disorders (gold standard for OCD)
mechanism: Habituation - anxiety naturally decreases with prolonged exposure; breaks anxiety-avoidance cycle; builds distress tolerance
steps: Work with therapist to identify specific fear (e.g., social situations, contamination, uncertainty)
Create 'exposure ladder' - list feared situations ranked by anxiety level (1-10)
Start with moderate anxiety situations (5-6 level)
Intentionally enter anxiety situation WITHOUT doing the compulsion (reassurance seeking, checking, avoidance)
Stay in situation for 20-45 min until anxiety naturally decreases (habituation curve)
Record: situation, anxiety level before/after, compulsion urges resisted
Repeat exposures; anxiety response weakens with practice
Gradually work up to higher-anxiety situations
benefits: Proven most effective for OCD and anxiety in youth
Increases freedom (less life organized around avoidance)
Superior to medication alone when combined
bestFor: Teens with specific phobias (social anxiety, heights, animals, contamination)
Those willing to tolerate temporary discomfort for lasting relief

name: CBT-I: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia
description: Evidence-based sleep intervention combining sleep restriction, stimulus control, sleep hygiene, and cognitive restructuring. Condensed for adolescents (4-6 sessions).
effectiveness: 75-80% for adolescent insomnia; each hour of sleep gained reduces depression by 11%
timeToEffect: 1-2 weeks for sleep improvement; 3-4 weeks for mood/anxiety improvement
mechanism: Improves sleep architecture and circadian rhythm regulation; secondary benefit to mood and anxiety via increased sleep
steps: Track sleep for 1 week: when do you go to bed, how long to fall asleep, how many times awake, when wake up?
Calculate your average sleep duration and 'sleep efficiency' (sleep time / time in bed)
Sleep Restriction: Start spending LESS time in bed (often counterintuitive!) - go to bed only when sleepy
Stimulus Control: Use bed ONLY for sleep/sex - no screens, studying, worrying in bed
Sleep Hygiene: No caffeine after 2pm, no screens 30-60 min before bed, consistent sleep schedule (±30 min)
Challenge sleep anxiety: 'Racing thoughts' and 'can't sleep' thoughts themselves keep you awake - notice them, don't fight
Keep tracking; gradually expand sleep window as efficiency improves (usually 2-4 weeks)
benefits: Directly improves sleep quality and duration
Secondary improvement in mood, anxiety, focus, immune function
Highly practical and self-directed (after initial assessment)
bestFor: Teens with insomnia or irregular sleep patterns
Those with depression/anxiety worsened by poor sleep
Can be used alongside all other treatments

name: Problem-Solving Therapy
description: Structured approach teaching youth to define problems clearly, generate solutions, evaluate options, implement, and learn. Highly practical for real-world teen challenges.
effectiveness: 65-70% for depression and anxiety related to stress; excellent for adjustment disorders
timeToEffect: 2-4 weeks to solve first problem; ongoing skill building
mechanism: Increases perceived control and agency; reduces rumination and helplessness; builds problem-solving efficacy
steps: Define the problem specifically (not 'I'm depressed' but 'I feel isolated because I haven't talked to friends in 2 weeks')
Brainstorm ALL possible solutions without judgment (even silly ones count)
For top 3 solutions, evaluate pros and cons realistically
Choose best solution (or combination)
Make concrete action plan: what, when, who, how?
Implement the plan
Evaluate: did it work? What would you do differently next time?
benefits: Builds sense of agency and control
Empowering for teens (they solve their own problems)
bestFor: Those stuck in rumination or 'nothing works' thinking
Prevention - can be taught in schools to all youth

name: Emotion Regulation Skills (DBT-Based)
description: Foundational DBT skills teaching emotion physiology, identification, and active regulation strategies. Essential for preventing crisis escalation.
effectiveness: 85% as part of full DBT; foundational for all emotional dysregulation
timeToEffect: 1-2 weeks to notice first skills working; mastery over 8-12 weeks
mechanism: Increases emotional awareness; builds distress tolerance and coping; prevents crisis escalation; reduces self-harm urges
steps: Learn emotion physiology: fight/flight/freeze response, how emotions live in body (chest, stomach, face)
Identify emotion triggers - events that start the feeling
Name emotions precisely (not just 'bad' - frustrated? disappointed? guilty? ashamed?)
ABC PLEASE: Attend to Physical needs first (eat, sleep, exercise, medications)
Check-in: What am I feeling right now, 0-10?
Choose regulation strategy: Opposite Action (do opposite of emotion urge - anxious → approach; angry → kind), or
Distress Tolerance: TIPP skills (Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation)
Track: What worked? Use again next time
benefits: Foundational skill for all emotional dysregulation
bestFor: Especially those with self-harm, anger, or anxiety
Can be taught in schools and clinical groups

name: Virtual Reality Exposure Therapy (VRET)
description: FDA-cleared VR environments for exposure therapy. Highly engaging for digital-native youth. Addresses social anxiety, phobias, and specific fears in controlled setting.
effectiveness: 71-80% comparable to in-vivo exposure; 95% engagement in youth
timeToEffect: 4-8 weeks; often faster than traditional exposure
mechanism: Safe habituation to feared situations; flexible, data-driven exposure; real-world practice built on VR foundation
steps: Work with therapist trained in VRET
Therapist guides setup of VR scenario matching your specific fear
Put on VR headset - immersion in safe simulation
Therapist adjusts difficulty in real-time (increase crowds, speaking time, etc.)
Practice staying in anxiety-provoking VR situation until anxiety decreases
Repeat sessions; transfer learning to real-world situations
Real-world homework between sessions
benefits: Data tracking of progress (therapist sees your anxiety curve)
Faster habituation for some than real-world exposure
bestFor: Social anxiety (public speaking, crowds, social situations)
toolsNeeded: VR headset (Meta Quest, Valve Index, HTC Vive)

name: Social Connection & Community Interventions
description: Structured approaches to address epidemic of youth loneliness through quality social connections. Evidence shows loneliness is 2.5x risk factor for depression/anxiety.
effectiveness: 58-72% for depression related to isolation; preventive benefit across all conditions
timeToEffect: 2-4 weeks to feel connection; 8-12 weeks for sustained benefit
mechanism: Reduces loneliness; increases sense of belonging; improves all mental health outcomes through social support
steps: Identify what kind of social connection appeals to you (1:1, small group, large group; activity-based, talk-based)
Explore options: clubs at school, community groups, online communities with moderation, meetups by interest
Start small: one low-pressure activity or group
Commit to showing up regularly (consistency builds connection)
Quality over quantity: one genuine friend better than 100 surface connections
Be curious about others: ask questions, listen
Notice how you feel before/after social contact
benefits: Builds sense of belonging and acceptance
bestFor: Those with depression/anxiety related to isolation

name: Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (ACT) - Youth Metaphors
description: Uses metaphors and experiential exercises to teach psychological flexibility. Teaches youth to make room for uncomfortable feelings while living aligned with values.
effectiveness: 70-75% for anxiety and depression; particularly strong for perfectionism
timeToEffect: 2-4 weeks for concepts; 8-12 weeks for behavior change
mechanism: Shifts from symptom-reduction to values-aligned living; builds psychological flexibility and distress tolerance
steps: Identify values: what matters most to you? (relationships, learning, creativity, adventure, integrity)
Notice your struggle with anxiety/worry: Try to fight it? Try to avoid it? How's that working?
'Leaves on Stream' exercise: imagine thoughts/feelings as leaves floating by - you don't grab them or push them away
'Expansion' exercise: instead of fighting anxiety, make room for it - breathe into it, say 'yes, this too'
Choose one value-aligned action THIS WEEK (even small) - do it despite anxiety
Notice: did the anxiety control you, or did you move toward what matters?
Repeat: values + committed action, regardless of feelings
benefits: Breaks 'try harder to feel better' cycle
Shifts focus from symptoms to meaningful living
bestFor: Teens caught in perfectionism or avoidance

name: Movement & Somatic Therapy
description: Uses body awareness, dance/movement, and grounding to process emotions stored physically. Highly effective for trauma, dissociation, and anxiety disconnection from body.
effectiveness: 62-70% for anxiety and depression; 65% improvement in body awareness
timeToEffect: 1-3 weeks for felt sense of relief; ongoing benefits with practice
mechanism: Releases stored trauma/tension; increases body awareness; activates parasympathetic nervous system
steps: Start with body scan: where do you feel tension? (chest, shoulders, stomach, jaw)
Slow, intentional movement: stretch that area gently, without forcing
Notice what feelings come up (anger, sadness, relief, nothing)
Dance or move authentically to music (no 'right way') - your body leads
Ground: feel your feet on floor, hands in your lap, weight in your seat
Notice: how do you feel after movement?
benefits: Releases physical tension and stored trauma
Increases body awareness and felt sense
Highly engaging; community aspect builds connection
Alternative to talk therapy for processing
bestFor: Those who move naturally or enjoy dance
Anxiety and depression with physical tension

name: Arts & Expressive Therapies
description: Non-verbal processing through art, music, drama, or writing. Particularly effective for trauma, grief, and emotions difficult to express in talk therapy.
effectiveness: 65-72% for depression and emotional expression; particularly strong for trauma
mechanism: Externalizes internal experience; builds agency through creation; processes without words; builds community
steps: Choose medium: visual art, music, writing, drama (no 'skill' needed)
Set intention: What feeling/experience are you expressing?
Create without judgment: this isn't about 'good art,' it's about expression
Share (optional) with trusted person or group
Reflect: What did you notice? What surprised you?
toolsNeeded: Art supplies, instrument, journal, or willingness
